newsitem.title: HONG KONG: PRESS DIGEST-Hong Kong Newspaper Editorials-June 6.
newsitem.headline: PRESS DIGEST-Hong Kong Newspaper Editorials-June 6.

text.p: There are 25 days to go before the British colony reverts to China. These are highlights of comments in the Hong Kong press. The views expressed are those of the newspapers quoted and do not represent an editorial viewpoint of Reuters.

-- ECONOMIC JOURNAL said the Official Secrets Bill recently passed by the Legislative Council threatened press freedom. The ironic part was that on the day the bill was discussed in the Legislative Council, all the members of the Democratic Party and the media were busy with the June 4 vigil, and the bill would not have been passed if several Democratic Party legislators had not been absent. The paper added that market competition was the best way to prevent self-censorship by the media.

-- The Beijing-funded TA KUNG PAO said the plan by members of the Democratic Party to challenge the legitamacy of the provisional legislature in court was a farce. It said the provisional legislature had been established according to the decisions of the National People's Congress and the Basic Law. While most Hong Kong people are looking forward to being real Chinese, some people missed the colonial system and wanted to turn the clock back, but they were doomed to fail, it said.

-- ECONOMIC TIMES said it was good news that China had started to care about its international image. It said many countries were observing China through what was happening in Hong Kong. So if Hong Kong's status quo, especially areas related to freedom, could be maintained, and the election of the first post-handover legislative body could be fair, open and democratic, China's image would be improved, the paper said.

-- HONGKONG STANDARD said that Ma Yuzhen, the new chief of China's Foreign Ministry Hong Kong office, would arrive in the territory with a deep understanding of the way things worked in both Hong Kong and Britain. The paper said that the appointment of Ma, who was now deputy director of the Information Office of the State Council, underlined the importance Beijing attached to Hong Kong's relationship with Britain.
